scams.name: Lakeside Pickpocketing
scams.description: Pickpockets work the crowds around Lake Annecy, the Palais de l’Ile, and the Old Town, usually in pairs or small teams. One person uses a distraction — asking for directions, staging a photo — while the other lifts wallets and phones. The lakefront promenade during the summer months sees the most incidents.
scams.avoidance: Use a cross-body bag with zipped compartments. Keep valuables in front pockets or inside jacket pockets. Stay alert in crowded areas. Never leave bags on chairs or the ground in restaurants.
scams.location: Lake Annecy promenade, Palais de l’Ile, Old Town (Vieille Ville), popular markets

scams.name: Beach Belongings Theft
scams.description: Thieves patrol the lakeshore beaches watching for swimmers who have left bags unattended on towels. They wait until you’re in the water or turned away, then scoop up wallet, phone, and keys and disappear into the crowd. Incidents spike during July and August at the busier beaches.
scams.avoidance: Never bring valuables to the beach. Leave jewelry and passports at your hotel. Use a waterproof pouch for essentials. Take turns swimming with companions so someone watches belongings.
scams.location: Plage d’Albigny, Plage des Marquisats, Plage de Talloires, all lakeside beaches

scams.name: Dual Menu Restaurant Scam
scams.description: Some restaurants in tourist areas maintain two sets of menus — one for locals with standard prices and another for tourists with inflated prices. Additionally, menus may lack prices entirely, only revealing exorbitant costs when the bill arrives. Hidden charges for bread, water, or cover fees may appear.
scams.avoidance: French law requires restaurants to display menus with prices outside. Ask for a menu with prices before ordering. Walk away from restaurants without posted prices. Verify the bill matches menu prices.
scams.location: Old Town restaurants near Palais de l’Ile, lakefront terraces, areas near major attractions

scams.name: Fake Petition and Charity Clipboard Scam
scams.description: Scammers approach tourists in the Old Town with clipboards asking for signatures on a petition for a charitable cause. After you sign, they demand a donation of €10–€20. The clipboard keeps your hands and eyes occupied while an accomplice works your bag from behind. The petitions feature photocopied logos from legitimate French charities — but the operation is entirely fraudulent.
scams.avoidance: Never stop for anyone with a clipboard. Say ‘Non merci’ firmly and keep walking. Keep hands on your belongings if approached. Legitimate charities do not solicit on streets with petitions.
scams.location: Old Town pedestrian areas, near major attractions, market areas, lakefront promenade

scams.name: The Gold Ring Trick
scams.description: A scammer ‘finds’ a gold ring on the ground near a tourist and asks if they dropped it. When the tourist says no, the scammer offers to sell it as a ‘lucky find’ for a significant sum, claiming it is valuable gold. The ring is worthless metal. This scam, common in Paris, occasionally appears in smaller French tourist towns.
scams.avoidance: Never engage with anyone claiming to find valuables near you. Say ‘Non’ and walk away immediately. Do not touch or examine anything offered.
scams.location: Pedestrian areas, lakefront, near tourist attractions

scams.name: Friendship Bracelet Scam
scams.description: Scammers aggressively approach tourists and begin tying a ‘friendship bracelet’ onto their wrist without permission. Once the bracelet is tied, they demand payment, often 10-20 euros or more, becoming aggressive if refused. While attempting to remove the bracelet, accomplices may pickpocket the distracted victim.
scams.avoidance: Keep your hands in pockets or crossed when walking. Never let strangers touch your hands or wrists. Walk away immediately saying ‘Non merci’ firmly.
scams.location: Pedestrian zones, Old Town, near popular photo spots

scams.name: Rental Car Break-ins
scams.description: Thieves target rental cars, easy to pick out by their license plates, missing floor mats, and sterile interiors. They smash windows to pull out luggage, electronics, and valuables, sometimes dropping the rear seats to get at the trunk. Parking at trailheads and scenic viewpoints above the lake is where most break-ins happen — exactly where you’ll want to stop on a day trip.
scams.avoidance: Never leave any valuables visible in your car. Remove all items including charging cables. Use staffed parking lots when available. Consider sedan rentals with proper trunks rather than hatchbacks.
scams.location: Trailhead parking areas, scenic viewpoints around the lake, unstaffed parking lots, street parking

scams.name: Vacation Rental Fraud
scams.description: Scammers create fake vacation rental listings for properties in Annecy that either do not exist or belong to someone else. Victims pay deposits or full amounts via bank transfer only to arrive and find no accommodation. Some scammers create sophisticated fake booking websites mimicking legitimate platforms.
scams.avoidance: Only book through official platforms like Airbnb or Booking.com. Never pay via bank transfer or cryptocurrency. Read reviews carefully. Verify property addresses on Google Maps.
scams.location: Online — affects pre-trip booking for Annecy accommodations

scams.name: ATM Skimming and Distraction
scams.description: Criminals install skimming devices on ATMs to capture card data and PINs. Others pose as helpful locals at ATMs or ticket machines, offering assistance while memorizing PIN codes or switching cards. An international ring was busted in 2025 after stealing over 580,000 euros across Western Europe.
scams.avoidance: Use ATMs inside banks during business hours. Cover the keypad completely when entering PINs. Decline help from strangers at ATMs. Check card slots for loose attachments before inserting cards.
scams.location: Standalone ATMs, tourist area cash machines, train station ticket machines

scams.name: Distraction Theft by Groups
scams.description: Thieves work in organized groups using distraction techniques. One person creates a diversion — asking for directions, showing a map, dropping items, staging an argument — while the others pick pockets and lift phones. They focus on tourists who are taking photos, consulting maps, or otherwise looking away from their own belongings.
scams.avoidance: Treat any unsolicited approach by a stranger, especially a group, as a probable setup. If someone creates a scene nearby, check your belongings first, then observe. Keep your phone and wallet in front pockets or a secured pouch. Travel with a companion who can watch your back when you’re framing a shot.
scams.location: Old Town, lakefront, popular photo spots, market areas, near the canal
